correctness.rationale: For fixed prime sets the Chinese remainder theorem gives independent geometric exact valuations (first truncate the allowed exponents); the omitted-prime mean is uniformly bounded by ∑_{p>P}p⁻² for integers up to X and for the independent-prime model. E Z_p=1/[p(p+1)], so the model sum is finite almost surely and the same tail bound gives weak convergence. Atomlessness also follows directly: distinct assignments of reciprocal powers or zero at a finite prime set have distinct sums, since multiplying their difference by the common denominator and reducing modulo a prime where the valuations differ leaves a nonzero residue. The largest possible mass of that finite sum is therefore ∏_{p≤P}(1−1/p)→0, an upper bound on the largest mass after adding the independent tail. Full support follows by greedily selecting reciprocals of sufficiently large primes to approximate any u≥0, imposing finitely many valuations (positive probability), then using Markov's inequality for the unassigned tail. In particular the CDF limit exists also at 0. For y→∞ the no-prime-through-y cylinder has mass M(y). Its independent tail has mean O(1/(y log y)) by the prime-counting upper bound and partial summation, giving relative loss O(1/log y). Conversely each p≤y must be absent or have valuation at least the first a with p^a≥y, a constraint of probability 1−1/p+p⁻ᵃ. Summing the exception terms contributes O(y⁻¹ᐟ²), by bounding each by 1/y through √y, each by p⁻² for √y<p<y, and treating prime y separately. Dividing their product by M(y) proves the matching relative bound. Mertens supplies e^(−γ); the CDF ratio is exactly the conditional logarithmic survival probability for fixed α≥1 and 0<t<1. This is an iterated endpoint limit after natural density, not a joint cutoff claim. The supplied finite checker was inspected but not run; the analytic proof covers the limits.

value.rationale: The normalized Erdős statistic is a natural arithmetic observable with a known general distribution-existence mechanism but no tail constant in that mechanism. Identifying the small-value frequency to sharp relative order explains quantitatively why rough-number avoidance dominates despite the possibility of small prime powers with high valuation. The conclusion is useful beyond finite examples and gives precise conditional thresholds as a consequence, without treating the Pareto rephrasing as a second contribution.
